historical_timeline.summary: Born Samuel Langhorne Clemens in Florida, Missouri.
Death of his son Langdon from diphtheria.
His publishing company fails; first attack of gout, in Paris, about this time.
Leaves on a worldwide lecture tour to repay his debts.
Death of his daughter Susy from meningitis.
Laid up with gout in Vienna.
Death of his wife near Florence.
Arrives for the summer at Dublin, New Hampshire.
A severe attack of gout in Norfolk, Connecticut.
First attacks of chest pain; told he has a "tobacco heart."
Dies at Stormfield of angina pectoris; his obituary says his losses had preyed upon his mind.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Prolonged grief disorder in a 69-year-old writer and humorist a year after his wife's death, after the earlier deaths of a son and a daughter. The episode covers the DSM-5-TR criteria and the PG-13-R; telling prolonged grief from normal grief and from major depression with the PHQ-9 and a clinical interview, and the decision not to start an antidepressant when major depression is absent; a structured safety assessment for passive thoughts of death in an older bereaved man, who is at high risk of suicide, with means safety and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; prolonged grief disorder therapy (Shear) in sixteen weekly sessions; sleep without sedative-hypnotics; tobacco use disorder in a cigar smoker since boyhood, with counseling and varenicline under the USPSTF recommendation; exertional chest tightness evaluated with an ECG and CT coronary angiography under the 1900 chest pain guideline, and nonobstructive coronary disease treated with a high-intensity statin and aspirin; gout with allopurinol started low and raised to a urate below 6 mg/dL, with colchicine prophylaxis and a flare treated without stopping allopurinol, under the ACR 1899 guideline; and social connection and his writing as part of recovery.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Clemens returns one week after intake and is seen by Dr. Ifeanyi-Strand of geriatric psychiatry on the same day. The nurse called him three days after intake; he had used his safety plan once, calling a friend on a bad evening. He still thinks of his wife many times a day, keeps her room as it was, and avoids the photograph albums; he says that part of him died with her and that his work seems pointless. consultant_note.history: Mr. Clemens, a 69-year-old writer and lecturer, is seen at the request of Dr. Achterberg-Lowe one week after intake. His wife died a year and two weeks ago after a long illness. He has lost a son and his eldest daughter in earlier years and says each loss "took a piece" but that this one took the rest. He thinks of her many times every day, feels that part of himself died with her, cannot believe at times that she is gone, avoids her photographs and the places they shared, feels intensely lonely, and finds his work meaningless. He sleeps four to five hours. He has passing wishes to join her but no intent or plan and has never tried to harm himself. Away from reminders his humor and curiosity return, and he does not regard himself as worthless. He has no history of mania or of psychiatric treatment. He drinks a glass of whisky most evenings and smokes about ten cigars a day
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Achterberg-Lowe's intake note and safety assessment. PHQ-9 11 (item 9 scored 1). PG-13-R 41 today. AUDIT-C 3. TSH 2.2 and vitamin B12 410, normal; hemoglobin A1c 5.8 percent; sodium and creatinine normal. ECG normal

assessment.assessment: More than twelve months after the death of someone close, he has daily yearning for and preoccupation with his wife, and at least three of the accessory symptoms (a sense that part of himself has died, disbelief, avoidance of reminders, intense emotional pain, difficulty taking up his life and work, meaninglessness and loneliness), lasting most days for at least the past month, beyond the norms of his community and culture, and impairing his work and friendships. This meets the DSM-5-TR criteria for prolonged grief disorder. The PG-13-R score of 41 agrees

Not present. The PHQ-9 of 11 reflects symptoms shared with grief; on interview his low mood is focused on the loss, his self-worth is intact, interest and humor return away from reminders, and he has fewer than five depressive symptoms. No antidepressant is advised now: in trials, prolonged grief disorder therapy works and an antidepressant added little to it except for depressive symptoms. Reconsider if major depression develops or the PHQ-9 rises

Prolonged grief disorder therapy (Shear), sixteen weekly sessions with a trained therapist: understanding grief, telling the story of the death, imaginal conversations with the deceased, memories, gradually revisiting avoided reminders, and rebuilding personal goals and relationships. His writing can be part of the goals work

Varenicline is the most effective single medicine for stopping smoking, and large trials found no rise in serious neuropsychiatric events, including in people with psychiatric illness. It is reasonable for him; mood, sleep and any thoughts of death should be checked at each visit
